- 300 agents writing and checking at the same time
- Every output verified against the source in ~100 ms
- Three passes over 100 company profiles → zero errors left
- Everything dumped straight into an Obsidian vault

The trick is the split: one model does the work, a cheaper one decides if the claim is actually true. The loop doesn’t stop until everything checks out

Art Deco didn't die from being exhausted, it got blacklisted.

Its three main phases - Zigzag, PWA / Stripped Classical, & Streamline - weren't exactly sequential, they overlapped all throughout the 30s. But what happened after 1929 wasn't just that zig zag Deco became too expensive, it was evolving from the 'Return to Order' (WW1) beginnings towards a more robust machine age adapted classicism. 

Earlier funding collapsed from private elites to the state, and a more civic form emerged - Stripped Classical/Classical Moderne. It was transatlantic, global. The American WPA, PWA, democracies and authoritarian regimes across the West all embraced it because the goal was the same: instill optimism, civic-mindedness, and resilience. Put your skilled artists & artisans to work.

It was seen as worthy recieving state funding for its public face - blending both classical & modern, a forward facing embrace between design, industry & craft.

That more colorful zig zag form was made logistically difficult to revive after 29, then that difficulty was made permanent. Deco needed a 50-year Beaux-Arts ecosystem - terracotta kilns like Gladding McBean and Atlantic Terra Cotta, plasterers, metal foundries, carvers, mosaicists - & that ecosystem took two hits. 

The 29 crash bankrupted the firms & dissolved the apprenticeship pipeline, then the war shifted what was left to war industries. By 1948 a fully crafted lobby was hard to build like 1926 even if you wanted to. 

Hard isnt impossible. With a regular cycle craft revives with demand, but revival was blocked. 

Tax codes, FAR, federal budgets, and curtain-wall specs all rewarded flat, uncrafted surfaces, so there wasnt much incentive to maintain the ateliers.

The firmest lockout was ideological. To make High Modernism the post-war approved standard, its promoters had to discredit what came before.

Politically, Stripped Classicism was rebranded as "fascistic" because Hitler, Mussolini and Stalin had used identical forms. Culturally Deco, especially Streamline, was the 1930s World's Fair spirit: mass-produced household objects made beautiful, futuristic, optimistic, commercial & everyday. 

High Modernism was austere, 'European' & highbrow, it treated that populist optimism as kitsch. That created a self-fulfilling loop: disincentivize the decorative, let craft firms die, then accuse dead craft as proof decorative design is infeasible. 

Hence the narrative that Deco simply "fell from public taste" is fake. 

It was slowed by the war, logistically hollowed out by '48, then ideologically blacklisted afterwards - making way for [indirect] tacit state support through modernist capture this time with the opposite design ethos: (mid century)"modernism".

The people never chose the glass modernist box over Deco. The people were simply never asked.
@oldbooksguy Simply moderne. 

"Jazz" is hindsight & it effectively ends with the 1929 crash. Classical Moderne thrives afterwards side by side with Streamline Moderne - the whole thing isnt stopped until late 1940s.

I can make 70% of humans yawn on command.

It started with a design mistake.

Back in 2023, I was designing Alora, a sleep music app, and accidentally deleted the eyes off its mascot. I was about to undo it, but for some reason I kept staring at it.

Now the entire expression had to come from just the mouth.

So we turned it into a slow yawn and made that the app’s opening animation.

And this is where it got interesting: yawning seems to be weirdly contagious.

Around 70% of people who watched the mascot yawn ended up yawning themselves.

We weren’t just showing someone sleepy anymore. We were making the person watching feel it too.

Still one of my favourite design accidents.

The decline of beauty in everyday life shows up in even the smallest things, like tickets, where we’ve let our obsession with efficiency win out over personality and artistic expression.

Like the ticket from the Guggenheim Museum in New York, which I've shared in the first photo. It's an iconic building that could have so easily inspired a beautiful ticket design, but they opted for the most economical option instead. 

Each example of this decline isn't a big deal, but the world becomes less charming and enchanted when people stop caring about craftsmanship. 

For some alternatives, scroll through the photos. The second one shows old Japanese train tickets, the third one shows an old circus ticket, and the fourth one is a World Series ticket from 2002, which felt magical when I got to hold one as an eight-year-old. 

So yes, there’s definitely been a decline. And maybe we’re okay with it! But it’s worth remembering that this decline isn’t inevitable. There is another way.

There is also the opposite in type design, that is extreme analytical approaches. Here is our custom Nelder-Mead solver that proposes Houston Mono chamfer nodes in ~2000 iterations. The goal is to smoothly transition from one direction to another using exactly 6 nodes with a 'smooth chamfer', i.e. two rounded 45 deg chamfer corners. 

Basically, I care about 3 components for Houston Mono chamfers:

1) How the stroke width smoothly changes from one thickness to another. Here the vertical stroke is 84. It transitions to horizontal at 80. But the midpoint of the chamfer is like ~85.63 (see the table)! It's not linear, but the solver makes this as even as possible.

2) How each of the 45 deg turns curve, i.e. curve tension. Held at 91% by the solver. That means the handles span 91% to the Tunni point (where two handles intersect).

3) How deep the chamfer is...O has deeper chamfers than 2 for example.

There are a few other things like I can bias/skew the stroke change as I see fit visually.
In type design, there are all these tools to help designers. For e.g., you can predefine specific stems (or autodetect) and set their values. So what happens is that the designer now follows these rigid rules and if they're violated, it's exactly like a linter/type checker. Errors are displayed on the screen. The designer tends to correct them, but soooo many times these rules just don't apply. It's a trap. The solution is to keep a printed sheet on your desk with ideal values and unliked from the software. Then nudge them as needed. Auto-hinting will suffer slightly but in vast majority of cases there is a higher priority of making the glyph look consistent with the rest of the typeface.

很喜欢这种把旅行照片收进田野笔记里的方式。
照片留住现场，旁边那枚略微缺墨的彩色橡皮章，只刻下最值得记住的轮廓。
树、穹顶、海岸都没有被讲满，反而像旅途中随手盖下的一页，安静，又很有地方感。

prompt：
请将我上传的每一张照片分别制作成一张独立的「橡皮章旅行田野笔记海报」，每张照片单独输出，不要多图拼贴。

整体采用4:3横版构图，将画面划分为左右两个区域，但不要绘制明显的分隔线。

左侧约占画面58%，忠实保留原始照片。准确保持主体身份、地形、建筑、植物、人物、空间关系、自然光影、真实质感和原有色彩氛围，仅进行克制的艺术出版物级摄影调色，并加入极轻微的细腻胶片颗粒。为适配版式可以自然裁切，但不得拉伸、扭曲、移动、替换或重新绘制主体。

右侧约占画面42%，使用温暖的米白色旧纸作为背景。纸张具有细微纤维、天然颗粒、轻微使用痕迹和哑光触感，同时保留大面积未经印刷的纸张留白，让空白成为版式的重要组成部分。

分析原始照片，从中提取最具地点辨识度的主体轮廓、建筑结构、地形走势、植物姿态、道路、水岸线或其他关键视觉关系，将其压缩成一枚小型多色橡皮章图像。

不要逐项复制照片中的全部内容。只保留能够让人一眼认出原始地点、主体和场景关系所必需的最少信息。删除人群、车辆、密集窗户、重复建筑、细碎植被、装饰构件和无关背景。

章印位于右侧纸张区域的中下部，整体只占右侧区域高度的约30%—38%，周围必须保留充足留白。章印不能放大成普通插画、完整风景画或品牌Logo。

根据原图构图决定章印的组织方式：

- 标志性建筑：保留最有辨识度的外轮廓、屋顶、穹顶、拱门、塔楼或主要结构。
- 山地聚落：将建筑压缩成沿地形排列的少量阶梯状色块。
- 海岸风景：保留山体走势、聚落层级、岸线和少量断续水纹。
- 城市远景：保留主要天际线、一个标志性建筑及一两层远山。
- 自然景观：保留主要山体、树木、水岸或道路的方向关系。
- 近景遮挡物：如果其对原图叙事重要，可作为前景章印轮廓保留。

从原始照片中提取2—4种专色油墨。优先使用炭黑、深绿、砖红、赭黄、灰蓝、灰褐等经过降低饱和度的颜色，但不得强行套用固定色盘。保留原照片最有辨识度的色彩性格，仅允许一个小面积颜色作为视觉强调。

每一种颜色都要呈现为分别手工盖印的效果：

真实橡皮章雕刻纹理、手工刻痕、粗细不均的排线、轮廓缺口、断裂边缘、干燥缺墨、纸张透底、颗粒状油墨、压力不均、局部重影，以及约1—2毫米的轻微套色偏移。

不同色层之间允许出现自然错位，边缘不能数字化平滑。印迹应像真正刻制后压在旧纸上的橡皮章，而不是套用滤镜的照片、平滑矢量插画或线稿Logo。

根据照片中的地点、主题和视觉意象生成文字：

地点英文名称
No. 编号
三个简短英文关键词
西元年份

文字放在章印下方或邻近留白处，使用小型、克制、略带机械误差的打字机字体。排版应像旅行者的田野记录，而不是广告标题。确保所有文字拼写准确，不添加无关标语、品牌或装饰性文案。

整体气质像建筑师、旅行作家或自然观察者保存的田野笔记：安静、克制、触感真实、地域明确、带有手工误差和收藏感。照片负责记录现场，章印负责留下记忆中最值得辨认的部分。

Avoid：明显的中央分隔线、圆形印章、中文红色印章、邮票齿孔、蜡封、贴纸拼贴、旅游纪念品模板、平滑矢量Logo、通用城市图标、完整复制所有建筑、密集刻画、儿童手工感、卡通风格、3D渲染、塑料质感、光滑数字渐变、过度饱和、过多文字、装饰堆积，以及重绘或改变左侧原始照片。

I was digging around the HyperCard 1.0.1 floppy image tonight, as one does, and found a curious private file: FONT 31756.

It's a font file containing all of the glyphs for HyperCard's tool palette, likely created by Kristee Kreitman and Marge Boots (credited in the app for Graphic Art).

I can't believe they were using this technique back in 1987, although it seems Bruce Tognazzini invented it with MouseText two years prior (!).

I was moved, as I often am by the work of our field's forebears, so created this little tool for everyone to explore it here:

readers were expected to manually type the listings into their sinclair to recreate the game. the source code flirts with graphic elements and gets woven into illustrations, occupying the same visual surface as its output. you understand “this code makes this world” before reading a single line. 

it makes me wonder what the modern equivalent of this would be, and part of why i don’t love working with a CLI or terminal, where the output lives on a different surface.

Thank you for taking the time to write this up — and for the pointer to your thesis; that figure is beautiful. You're right that classical sphere inversion is exactly the starting point: the feature is named "Sphere Inversion" in the tool for that reason. "Inversphere" is the name of the resulting object, not a claim of new mathematics.

I should say up front that I'm not a mathematician, so please correct me if I get any of this wrong. My motivation was visual rather than mathematical: with the classical map, the entire far field piles up into a dense blob at the center (10× farther ⇒ 10× closer), and I simply wanted to control that density to balance the look of the finished object.

 To do that, the radial profile is generalized to f(r) = R·h(v), where v = (R/r − R/D)/(1 − R/D) is a normalized inverted depth and h is a μ-law log compression, h(v) = ln(1+μv)/ln(1+μ). Classical R²/r is the special case μ = 0, D = ∞. The footage here uses μ > 0, so — as far as I can tell — the map shown is outside the conformal family: the tangential scale f/r and radial scale |f′| agree only in the classical limit. If I understand Liouville's theorem correctly, this trade-off was unavoidable: staying conformal in 3D leaves no freedom to adjust the density, so angle preservation is given up deliberately in exchange for control over it. With μ > 0, mid-field depth below the sphere surface grows like log r, so distant scenery layers logarithmically inside the sphere.

 The 3DGS side also needed some care: each splat's covariance is carried by the Jacobian J = s·I + (f′−s)nnᵀ, depth sorting has to be re-keyed because inversion reverses the radial order, and the on/off transition is a linear blend whose Jacobian is exactly mix(I, J, t).

 Thanks again for taking the time — an expert eye on this is very welcome.
Since nobody called it out in the comments, this “new way” to show 3D Gaussian splats is a basic 19th century construction, studied by Jakob Steiner and others, called a “sphere inversion” or “Möbius transformation”:

https://t.co/R2t6Kho3TP

It looks good because it is an example of a so-called conformal map, which preserves angles, but distorts scales.  However, when you look at something up close, it doesn't really matter what its absolute scale is (whereas angular distortion is far more noticeable).

Conformal maps, namely the 16th century Mercator projection (old as it is) remains the projection of choice in Google Maps and other mapping tools, since it is the unique map that (i) preserves angles, and (ii) keeps north pointing "up" everywhere on the globe.

The 3DGS scheme shown here is just bumping up the usual approach up one dimension: apply a conformal projection; keep the "up" direction fixed.  The specific choice of conformal maps (inversions in the sphere) are in fact the only choice available in 3D, due to Liouville's theorem on conformal mappings.

[Orange illustration below is from my PhD thesis on conformal geometry: https://t.co/5yANJzFfjD]

フィラデルフィア・ワイヤーマンは、1982年にフィラデルフィアの路上に捨てられていた1,200点もの作品群の作者につけられた呼称である。作者の正体は現在も不明のままだが、ワイヤーを自在に曲げ、固く締め上げるための身体能力から男性であると推測され、発見地域の人口統計学的特徴や作品が持つ呪術的なアニミズム的側面から、アフリカ系アメリカ人の人物であると考えられている。
発見された作品群は、プラスチックの破片や日用品、電池、電気回路といった都市の「残骸」を、無数のワイヤーで幾重にも巻き付けた小品であった。それらは単なる廃棄物の集合体ではなく、一つひとつがまるで何らかの儀式的な目的を持っているかのように、執拗かつ緻密に構成されている。素材の異質さと、それを束ねるワイヤーの緊張感は、見る者に「これは何のための封印なのか」「あるいは何を繋ぎ止めるための装置なのか」という根源的な問いを突きつける。
これらの作品が大量かつ一箇所に遺棄されていた事実は、作者の死、あるいは深刻な生活環境の変化を強く示唆している。生涯を通じて人知れずこれらを制作し続けた作者にとって、これらのオブジェクトは、壊れた日常や社会の片隅で溢れ出す記憶を、物理的に「固定」するための唯一の手段であったのかもしれない。捨て去られた1,200点の彫刻は、街のゴミ集積場という無機質な場所を、突如として一個人の精神の記録庫へと変貌させた。
現在、これらの遺物は世界的な美術館に収蔵され、アウトサイダー・アートの重要な一翼を担っている。しかし、作者の名前は依然として「ワイヤーマン」という匿名の肩書きの中に埋もれたままだ。社会的な記録から完全に零れ落ちた人物が、これほどまでに強烈な「個」の痕跡を残したという事実は、現代の私たちが忘却しがちな、表現が持つ剥き出しの強度を現代に突きつけている。

光はモネから、
色の組み立てはスーラから。

現在制作中のZETA。
まだ頭部と胸部だけですが、今回の光と色の方向が、ようやく見えてきました。

光について参考にしているのは、モネの夕景です。
左から差し込む暖かな光が、装甲の固有色を強く染める。
その一方で、反対側には冷たい空気光を残しています。

青い装甲だからといって、青だけで作っているわけではありません。
黄、橙、青緑、紫——
異なる色を細かな筆触として並べ、距離の中で一つの青に見せています。

色の作り方は、スーラの点描から。
ただし、絵画の「点」をそのまま再現するのではなく、
装甲の面と流れに合わせて、短い筆触へ置き換えています。

近づけば、色は一つずつ分かれて見える。
少し離れると、それが光になる。

モネの光と、スーラの色彩理論。
二つの異なる絵画言語を、一つの立体表面の上で統合する試みです。

まだ上半身の途中。
ここから、この光を全身へどう連続させるかを探っていきます。

WINDOWS // NYC 

For the past five years, I've immersed myself in a photographic, typological study of the illuminated windows of New York City at night. On June 16th, we invite you to build a new world with us, a multilayered, interconnected city of light and shadow, powered by @TransientLabs Studio. 

This has been my biggest undertaking to date, and is the extension of my lifelong interest in photographic patterns and generative photography. This interest was crystalized in 2021 with my project DRIVE and continued in 2022 with Drip Drop. 

Over the years, I've learned so much about the conceptual world of typologies, about the intersection of photographic technologies and blockchain as immutable records of consensus and truth, and of course, about how the constant evolution of technology broadens the scope of what is possible for us artists- revealing new ways to create and connect with the people who seek to do the same. 

The process of creating WINDOWS // NYC has been the best sort of challenge, and as always, the incredible minds at @TransientLabs have taken my ideas and built technological frameworks that have elevated this project beyond my wildest dreams. I cannot wait to show you more, but for now, drop a comment if you want to connect, hear what we've built, and for information on how to participate and get involved. 

I love this world. I love looking at it in intricate detail and making photographs so that others can look at it that way too. And this pattern of windows and grids is one of my favorite ways to see. 

Sign up at windows dot davekrugman dot com, or via link in the comments below!

Engineering is the highest form of Art

… and it isn’t even close.

The items below are all exquisite pieces, each for completely different reasons. But each one a game changer in their own domain.

It’s difficult to get across the level of effort that was poured into each of these but they represent millions of hours of hard work, from the most competent people a society can muster.

This is what par excellence looks like in the domain of exquisite hardware.

However… the age of exquisite might be ending.

It’s not crazy to consider that the high water mark of exquisite hardware is already behind us?

In the future we might be much more focused on the unit economics and the machine that makes the machine, rather than product itself.

This will fundamentally change what society builds, and how such articles are perceived.

You might be forever telling kids “they don’t make things how they used to” and this tike it might be true.

Not everywhere, but in enough places that it’s recognised as a generalised industrial trend.

Last year, we invested in @Monumental_Labs.

They use AI and robotics to reduce the cost of stone fabrication by 90%. 

Construction tech is our game and while I think what they are doing with art and sculpture fab is amazing, the bull case for ML imo was doing building scale construction with stone. Essentially, reviving a dormant material type for type I construction to compete directly with steel and concrete.

Before investing, I had to answer a question that's been nagging me for years: exactly when and why did we stop building with natural materials like stone? Where did beauty in our built environment go to die?

It's mostly always been an economic story.

I’m using a two-engine setup lately. Three.js handles the real 3D space and depth, then I pass that depth info into p5.js to draw. The right side looks 3D, but it’s actually all flat 2D drawing. That’s the fun part. I can render the brush strokes in pure 2D so the lines feel more hand-drawn, while still keeping proper depth and overlap.
In short, Three.js does the space. p5.js does the drawing feel.

In 1991, the retreating Iraqi army set over 600 oil wells on fire in Kuwait, creating a landscape that looked like the end of the world. This isn’t CGI or a sci-fi movie, it’s real footage. Director Werner Herzog didn’t film it like a normal news report; he filmed it like an alien planet. There are no interviews and no politics, just the terrifying, massive scale of a planet burning. It’s a haunting reminder of what we’re capable of doing to the Earth.

Karateka, released in 1984 for the Apple II by Jordan Mechner (while he was a Yale student!), stood out as a groundbreaking title for its era. My biggest achievement as a student was getting out of bed in time for the majority (not all) classes...

The innovations included pioneering rotoscoped animation, where Mechner filmed himself performing karate moves on video, traced the frames by hand, and digitized them frame-by-frame for ultra-fluid, lifelike character movements.

It was also one of the first games to use cinematic storytelling scenes, inspired by Akira Kurosawa films, and silent movies: wordless cutscenes with cross-cutting (such as showing the princess in peril or the villain's reactions), dramatic pauses and tracking shots.

Mechner also had a sense of humor: The Apple II disk included an Easter egg: the game was single-sided but when you flipped the disk it would pay the game the full game upside-down and mirrored, causing players to call tech support in confusion.

The Vanguard-Cheetah XR7 combines the biological grace and speed of a cheetah with cutting-edge robotics. Its lightweight exoskeletal frame is built from a nano-alloy composite, providing durability without compromising agility. The internal musculature system, powered by synthetic myofibers, mimics the explosive power of a real cheetah, enabling bursts of speed up to 150 km/h in optimal conditions.

The XR7’s neural core is an advanced AI system capable of terrain mapping, autonomous decision-making, and target recognition. Embedded within its sleek design are modular tools for specialized missions, including life detection sensors and environmental samplers.

Advanced Features:

-HyperKinetic Actuators: These actuators provide near-instantaneous acceleration, allowing the XR7 to traverse rough terrain, climb obstacles, and perform agile maneuvers.
-Adaptive Skin Layer: A semi-transparent outer layer with embedded sensors that regulate temperature and detect environmental hazards.
-ThermoCore Power Unit: A compact reactor that uses thermoelectric conversion to generate power from environmental heat sources, ensuring prolonged operation in remote regions.
-VisionNet Suite: A multi-spectrum vision system capable of detecting infrared, ultraviolet, and electromagnetic signals for locating hidden objects or lifeforms.
-Biomechanical Tail Stabilizer: A dynamic tail that enhances stability and maneuverability during high-speed chases or sudden directional changes.
Mission Applications:

-Search and Rescue: The XR7 can navigate disaster zones to locate survivors, deliver supplies, and map hazardous areas.
-Environmental Monitoring: Equipped with biosensors, it tracks wildlife movements, measures air and soil quality, and identifies illegal deforestation or poaching activity.
-Security and Surveillance: Its stealth capabilities and rapid mobility make it ideal for patrolling large facilities or borders.
-Scientific Exploration: The XR7’s ability to cover vast terrains quickly makes it an asset in mapping ecosystems, studying migration patterns, and conducting biodiversity assessments.

Legacy:
The Vanguard-Cheetah XR7 is a testament to Salt x Diamond Corp.’s vision of engineering solutions that coexist with nature. Though its sleek, cybernetic appearance evokes technological superiority, its core mission is deeply rooted in preserving and protecting the natural world.

The XR7’s tagline, "Speed for Survival," underscores its dual purpose as both a defender of life and an explorer of the unknown.

古典的な幾何学的錯視の例。（a）ミュラー=リヤー錯視。上下の水平線分は同じ長さであるが、下の方が長く見える。（b）エビングハウス錯視。リングの中の円は左右同じ大きさであるが、大きい円のリングに囲まれた左の円よりも、小さい円のリングに囲まれた右の円の方が大きく見える。（c）ポンゾ錯視。Λや＜の頂点に近い方に置かれた対象が大きく見える。具体的には、2本の水平線分は同じ長さだが、上の方が長く見える。2つの円は同じ大きさだが、左の方が大きく見える。（d）ポッゲンドルフ錯視。2つの斜線は一直線上にあるが、右の斜線の方が上方に変位して見える。（e）ツェルナー錯視。垂直より反時計回りに45度傾いた黒い線は互いに平行だが、交互に傾いて見える。交差する短い線との交差角度の過大視の現象である。（f）へリング錯視（湾曲錯視）。水平線分が曲がって見える。上の線分は上に凸、下の線分は下に凸に見える。（g）ミュンスターベルク錯視。白と黒の正方形の列を図のようにずらして配置し、列の境界に線分を描くと、図ではそれらは水平であるが、交互に傾いて見える。本図のように線が灰色の時は、カフェウォール錯視（Café Wall illusion）と呼ばれることが多い。（h）フレーザー錯視。垂直より反時計回りに45度傾いた仮想線に沿って短い斜線の列が描かれているが、列の傾きは短い斜線の傾きの方向に変位して見える。ツェルナー錯視とは逆の錯視である。（i）フレーザー錯視の渦巻き錯視。フレーザー錯視では、傾いて見えるのは線分であるが、傾いて見える対象を円状に配置した時に観察できる錯視である。具体的には、同心円が渦巻きのように見える。
